section_summary: This section begins with the continuation of a detailed interview of Rockefeller laboratory technician Glasounoff about an unidentified man’s attempt to bribe him for the virulent Asibi strain of yellow fever virus. Supporting statements and correspondence connect the approach to Japanese Army bacteriologist Dr. Ryoichi Naito’s recent, unsuccessful official request for the same virus, while State Department officials debate surveillance, diplomatic action, and wartime precautions. The remaining records concern suspected Japanese agents and intelligence activities, including Galina Rosling, Japanese fishing interests in California and Mexico, Sehei Ono, Jesse Shima, Shintaro Fukushima, T. Hattori, J. Takeda, and Seattle importer C. T. Takahashi.

subfiles.title: Continuation of Glasounoff interview concerning the attempted theft of yellow-fever virus
subfiles.to: Rockefeller Foundation investigators, including Mr. Fosdick
subfiles.about: Glasounoff describes his background, laboratory access, and an unidentified man’s attempt to bribe him for the Asibi strain of yellow-fever virus.
subfiles.summary: The questioning reviews Glasounoff’s work for the Rockefeller Foundation in West Africa and New York, his duties in the yellow-fever animal house, and his movements on Sunday, February 26, 1939. He recounts being directed to a meeting near Exterior Street, where a well-dressed stranger offered as much as $3,000 for virulent Asibi virus and explained how Glasounoff could obtain it from an infected monkey while working alone. After repeated refusals, the stranger seized Glasounoff’s ignition key and warned him to forget the encounter; Glasounoff then reported the incident to Drs. Theiler and Bauer. Glasounoff speculates that the virus might be intended for murder or large-scale contamination but says he cannot identify the motive.

subfiles.title: Statement of J. H. Bauer on Glasounoff’s report
subfiles.about: Bauer records Glasounoff’s first report of the approach and the Rockefeller officials’ initial deliberations over notifying police.
subfiles.summary: Bauer states that Glasounoff arrived at his apartment on February 26 and described both the preliminary approach at York Avenue and the subsequent demand for Asibi virus. The stranger allegedly offered $3,000, suggested bleeding and desiccating material from an infected monkey, physically restrained Glasounoff, and took his ignition key. Bauer consulted Sawyer, Gasser, Rivers, and Smith; because police involvement might produce publicity and Glasounoff lacked a license number, they deferred action until Monday.

subfiles.title: Statement of J. H. Bauer on Dr. Ryoichi Naito’s request
subfiles.about: Bauer describes Naito’s official request for vaccine and virulent yellow-fever strains immediately before the attempted bribery.
subfiles.summary: Bauer says Naito presented a Japanese Embassy introduction and requested both the vaccine strain and unmodified Asibi virus for the Tokyo Institute of Infectious Diseases. Sawyer refused because Far Eastern health authorities opposed introducing yellow-fever virus into Asia. Naito continued asking about vaccines and said he had studied leptospires at the Robert Koch Institute before an anticipated posting to active duty.

subfiles.title: Statement of Dr. C. M. MacLeod
subfiles.about: MacLeod recounts Naito’s November 1938 tour of the Rockefeller Institute Hospital and his scientific questions.
subfiles.summary: MacLeod spent about two hours showing Naito the hospital and discussing pneumonia work, including the media room for pneumococcus broth. Naito described research on the differential diagnosis of Weil’s disease and yellow fever but displayed only perfunctory interest in most hospital work. He did not request access to the yellow-fever laboratories and later sent a courteous letter of thanks.

subfiles.title: Statement of W. A. Sawyer, Director of the International Health Division
subfiles.about: Sawyer explains why he refused Naito’s February 23 request to take virulent yellow-fever virus to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Bauer informed Sawyer that Naito had arrived with Yamauti’s letter and requested laboratory demonstrations and virulent virus. After consulting Rivers, Sawyer refused, citing the danger of introducing yellow fever into Asia and the 1930 League of Nations health recommendations. Naito accepted the decision, asked for written confirmation, and returned to the laboratory to complete his visit.

subfiles.title: Sawyer letter refusing Naito’s virus request
subfiles.about: Sawyer formally confirms that the Rockefeller Foundation will not supply virulent yellow-fever virus for transport to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Sawyer acknowledges that the request originated with the superintendent of Tokyo’s Government Institute of Infectious Diseases and was supported by Colonel Yamauti. He says Rockefeller policy and the League of Nations advisory opinion preclude sending living virulent virus to the Far East, while offering to help investigate scientific questions within Rockefeller’s own laboratory.

subfiles.title: Rivers letter to Gasser on accommodating Naito
subfiles.about: Rivers advises that Naito cannot work in Avery’s laboratory but may make a one-day hospital visit.
subfiles.summary: Rivers and Avery consider a several-month placement impossible because Institute policy disfavors short-term observers and no laboratory space is available. Avery nevertheless offers a day’s visit, with Colin MacLeod assigned to show Naito the hospital and laboratory.

subfiles.title: Gasser letter to Yamauti limiting Naito to a visit
subfiles.about: Gasser rejects a laboratory appointment for Naito but offers a tour of the Rockefeller hospital.
subfiles.summary: Gasser explains that volunteer workers require formal invitations and normally join laboratories for extended periods arranged well in advance. Avery’s laboratory already has too many voluntary workers, so Naito cannot be added even on a long-term basis. Rivers will instead arrange a visit on November 28 or 29.

subfiles.title: Gasser referral of Yamauti’s request to Rivers
subfiles.about: Gasser asks Rivers whether Naito can spend two months in the hospital department or at least receive a one-day visit.
subfiles.summary: Gasser forwards his correspondence with Colonel Yamauti for Rivers’s consideration. He asks whether Avery or colleagues might host Naito for two months and, failing that, whether the hospital could welcome him for a day.

subfiles.title: Gasser’s initial refusal of Naito’s two-month study request
subfiles.about: Gasser declines Yamauti’s request that Naito study bacteriology at the Rockefeller Institute for two months.
subfiles.summary: Gasser explains that the Institute is not organized to give outsiders a short general survey of science. Its scientists are appointed to specific laboratories for at least a year, so it cannot accept Naito for the proposed period beginning November 21.

subfiles.title: State Department warning to the Secretary of the Navy about Japanese interest in yellow-fever virus
subfiles.from: A. A. Berle Jr., for the Secretary of State
subfiles.to: Frank Knox, Secretary of the Navy
subfiles.about: The State Department alerts the Navy to Naito’s 1939 request and the subsequent bribery attempt as a possible biological threat.
subfiles.summary: The letter recounts Yamauti’s introduction of Naito, the Rockefeller Institute’s refusal to provide a virulent strain, and the nearly immediate offer of a $3,000 bribe to an Institute employee. Rockefeller scientists reportedly warned that yellow fever could spread catastrophically in mosquito-bearing areas of China, although no virus was missing from their stock. In the wartime situation, the Navy is invited to consider protective measures, with strict confidentiality requested.

subfiles.title: State Department warning to the Secretary of War about Japanese interest in yellow-fever virus
subfiles.from: A. A. Berle Jr., for the Secretary of State
subfiles.to: Henry L. Stimson, Secretary of War
subfiles.about: The State Department sends the War Department the same confidential warning about Japan’s possible acquisition of yellow-fever virus.
subfiles.summary: The letter reviews Naito’s Rockefeller contacts, the refusal to furnish virus, and the ensuing bribery attempt against a trusted laboratory employee. It notes Rockefeller scientists’ concern that introducing the virus into mosquito-infested China could cause a violent epidemic and acknowledges that Japan might have obtained virus elsewhere. The communication recommends strict secrecy and consideration of protective measures.

subfiles.title: Berle memorandum proposing notification of the War and Navy Departments
subfiles.about: Berle suggests revisiting the 1939 yellow-fever incident and warning the military departments.
subfiles.summary: Berle observes that Japanese doctors failed to secure yellow-fever virus from Rockefeller but may have obtained it elsewhere. He proposes bringing the incident to the attention of the War and Navy Departments so that protective measures can be considered.

subfiles.title: American Embassy London memorandum on Galina Pavlovna Rosling
subfiles.about: The Embassy requests information about Galina Rosling, a traveler suspected by a reliable source of being a Japanese agent.
subfiles.summary: Rosling, wife of a Royal Army Service Corps driver in Tientsin, sailed from Kobe to San Francisco aboard the Tatsuta Maru. Although reportedly without independent means, she had traveled to Manila and Singapore. The British source asks for any available information because she may be acting for Japan.

subfiles.title: Memorandum reporting the investigation of Galina Rosling
subfiles.about: The memorandum summarizes immigration and investigative information about Galina Rosling after her arrival in San Francisco.
subfiles.summary: Rosling declared that she came for a six-month visit to see friends, obtain a divorce, and eventually become an American citizen. Investigators found no definite espionage activity and considered her mentally unbalanced, but noted inconsistencies concerning her finances, husband, former partner Sergeant Sheldon, and an expected inheritance from Harbin. Her request to extend her stay was denied, and officials expected her to leave the country soon.

subfiles.title: Note to Messersmith concerning an informal search
subfiles.about: The writer advises Messersmith that the contemplated search can be made at any time without formality.
subfiles.summary: The brief note responds to a matter Messersmith raised that morning. In the surrounding context, it apparently concerns the possible search associated with the Naito investigation, though the page itself does not identify the person to be searched.

subfiles.title: Fosdick letter forwarding Naito correspondence
subfiles.about: Fosdick sends photostats of two letters mailed by Naito from San Francisco.
subfiles.summary: One enclosure was addressed to Sawyer and referred to Sawyer’s February 23 refusal to provide the virus; the other was addressed to Bauer. Fosdick promises to inform Messersmith immediately if further information develops.

subfiles.title: Messersmith reply to Fosdick on the Naito investigation
subfiles.about: Messersmith acknowledges the Naito letters and says the State Department continues to suspect a sinister purpose.
subfiles.summary: Messersmith thanks Fosdick for the photostats and promises to keep Rockefeller informed of any Departmental action. He states that officials cannot dismiss the possibility of a sinister purpose behind Naito’s efforts to obtain the virus and his contacts with trusted employees.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs recommendations on the Naito incident
subfiles.about: Far Eastern Affairs recommends against a diplomatic approach to Japan while favoring confidential consultation with military intelligence.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum concludes that Yamauti’s letters were courteous and that Japan could plausibly defend the request on scientific grounds, especially because Formosa had yellow-fever vectors and Japan and China were not expressly covered by the League opinion. A diplomatic protest or search might merely put Japan on guard and drive any acquisition effort underground. The authors recommend no approach to Japan, Britain, or France, but propose reviewing Labor Department records and briefing senior MID and ONI officers.

subfiles.title: Draft memorandum requesting Japan’s reasons for seeking yellow-fever virus
subfiles.about: The draft summarizes Naito’s requests and asks why Japanese institutions wanted virulent yellow-fever virus.
subfiles.summary: The draft recounts Yamauti’s letters, Naito’s proposed study, and Rockefeller’s refusal based on institutional policy and epidemic danger. It emphasizes the absence of yellow fever in Japan, the presence of vectors in southern China, and the risk of a disastrous Asian epidemic. It would ask the Japanese government to explain the intended purpose of the virus.

subfiles.title: Messersmith memorandum closing the Naito file
subfiles.about: Messersmith agrees that no immediate action is useful but calls for broader rules governing diplomatic missions’ contacts.
subfiles.summary: Messersmith accepts Hornbeck and Hamilton’s recommendation to place the case in the confidential files. He nevertheless urges a future review of how foreign diplomatic personnel approach U.S. agencies and private organizations, and of corresponding instructions for American missions abroad.

subfiles.title: Receipt for ONI report Com-11 serial no. 305
subfiles.about: The Department acknowledges receipt of a confidential San Diego report on Japanese activities.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum lists Com-11 serial number 305, dated March 21, 1939, from San Diego. It instructs that the signed original receipt be returned to the Office of Naval Intelligence.

subfiles.title: Com-11 report: Activities of Japanese
subfiles.to: Office of Naval Intelligence and Department of State
subfiles.about: The report forwards allegations concerning Japanese-associated businesses, fishermen, and shipping in Southern California and the Gulf of California.
subfiles.summary: The source recommends scrutiny of Tanklage, Kuwabara, Kondo, and Wakayama and reports a transfer of frozen shrimp between the Sendai Maru and Minowo Maru. It describes Japanese dominance of the Gulf of California shrimp fishery and Mexican efforts to reserve fishing for Mexican citizens or cooperatives. The report warns that cancellation of Japanese fishing contracts might provoke a serious Japanese-Mexican dispute.

subfiles.title: Messersmith letter acknowledging the Sehei Ono report
subfiles.from: George S. Messersmith, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Messersmith acknowledges the FBI report on Sehei Ono and requests future reports in the case.
subfiles.summary: The Department confirms receipt of Hoover’s May 10 letter and Special Agent J. P. MacFarland’s report concerning Sehei Ono. Messersmith asks the FBI to forward copies of any subsequent reports.

subfiles.title: Internal memorandum on Sehei Ono and Takahashi
subfiles.about: The memorandum proposes coordinating FBI, postal-inspector, ONI, and MID information concerning Ono and Takahashi.
subfiles.summary: The writer says the Department has no information on Ono but possesses Takahashi material obtained from postal inspectors in Seattle and Denver. He suggests that the relevant agents contact those inspectors and that ONI and MID receive copies of the Ono report. A handwritten annotation records that the responsible official agreed to make contact.

subfiles.title: FBI file-return notice
subfiles.from: Department of State Office of Security
subfiles.about: The slip records the return of a letter and its enclosures to the FBI.
subfiles.summary: The document is an administrative file-control notice. It states that the material bearing the indicated file number was returned through the Office of Security.

subfiles.title: Second FBI file-return notice
subfiles.from: Department of State Office of Security
subfiles.about: A second slip records the return of another letter and its enclosures to the FBI.
subfiles.summary: This is another administrative notice using substantially the same wording as the preceding page. It confirms return of the referenced file material via the Office of Security.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs memorandum distinguishing Fukushima from Jesse Shima
subfiles.about: The memorandum rejects an allegation that diplomat Shintaro Fukushima was identical with alleged spy Jesse S. Shima.
subfiles.summary: Mr. Salisbury had known Fukushima since 1932 in Washington, Tokyo, and New York and considered him an able, outspoken younger diplomat. On that basis, Far Eastern Affairs concludes that the identification resulted from confused identities and that Fukushima was not engaged in activity incompatible with his diplomatic post. The division had no information about the other people in the attached file.

subfiles.title: Request for information on Shima, Fukushima, and Dixon
subfiles.from: Mr. Warren, Office of the Assistant Secretary
subfiles.about: Warren requests all available information on four people named in an espionage inquiry.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum asks Far Eastern Affairs for material on J. S. Shima, Sabretta Shima, Shintaro Fukushima, and Marion Dixon. It is an internal search request preceding the Department’s reply to the FBI.

subfiles.title: Messersmith response to Hoover on the Jesse Shima case
subfiles.from: George S. Messersmith, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department reports that its only relevant information concerns Fukushima and denies that he is Jesse Shima.
subfiles.summary: The Department acknowledges the FBI report titled “Jesse B. Shima; Japanese Spy Ring—Espionage.” Its files contain no information about the named individuals except Shintaro Fukushima, a Japanese diplomatic secretary personally known to a Department officer. Messersmith states that Fukushima is not Jesse Shima and is not believed to be engaged in improper activities, while requesting future FBI information.

subfiles.title: FBI file-return notice for the Shima case
subfiles.from: Department of State Office of Security
subfiles.about: The slip records the later return of the Shima-case letter and enclosures to the FBI.
subfiles.summary: The page is an administrative file-return form. It states that the letter and enclosures bearing the file number were returned through the Office of Security.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs response concerning unidentified persons
subfiles.about: Far Eastern Affairs reports that it has no knowledge of the people named in an attached investigative file.
subfiles.summary: The response is brief and categorical. It advises Warren that none of the persons mentioned in the attached material are known to the division.

subfiles.title: Request to Far Eastern Affairs concerning persons in an attached file
subfiles.from: Mr. Warren, Office of the Assistant Secretary
subfiles.about: Warren asks whether Far Eastern Affairs knows anything about the people named in an attached espionage file.
subfiles.summary: The handwritten routing memorandum requests a check of the division’s knowledge. In context, it belongs to the correspondence that produced the negative response and the subsequent Hattori-Takeda letter to the FBI.

subfiles.title: Messersmith acknowledgment of the Hattori-Takeda espionage report
subfiles.from: George S. Messersmith, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Messersmith acknowledges an FBI report on T. Hattori and J. Takeda and reports that State Department files contain no information.
subfiles.summary: The Department confirms receipt of the investigative report titled “T. Hattori; J. Takede; Espionage.” A file search disclosed nothing about the persons named, and Messersmith asks Hoover to continue sending reports in the case.

subfiles.title: Special Agent memorandum forwarding Takahashi inquiries
subfiles.from: R. C. Bannerman, Office of the Chief Special Agent
subfiles.about: The memorandum forwards reports concerning what Takahashi sought from George Jenison and Takahashi’s standing in Seattle.
subfiles.summary: The inquiry was intended to determine the information Takahashi requested from Jenison. It also sought an assessment of Takahashi’s relative importance in Seattle, and the writer forwards two reports as potentially useful.

subfiles.title: Preliminary postal-inspector report on C. T. Takahashi
subfiles.from: S. H. Morse, Post Office Department Inspector
subfiles.about: Morse provides preliminary information on Seattle importer C. T. Takahashi and his reputation and activities.
subfiles.summary: The report identifies Takahashi as an importer-exporter dealing extensively in scrap iron and rubber shipped to Japan and notes that he had recently returned from Japan. Other sources portray him as active in fishing, gambling, racketeering, mining, and speculative transactions, and say that some Japanese regarded him as a “killer.” The letter continues beyond this section after beginning to discuss his former associate Yamamoto.
